problem: End-to-end visuomotor/VLN policies trained from pixels and language generalize poorly because they learn environment-specific correlations, and action-level distillation from privileged experts is ambiguous and entangles perception with control.
motivation: Control depends on compact geometric quantities (goal direction, obstacle proximity), while perception must infer them from RGB and language. Decoupling the two and aligning perception to a fixed expert latent gives dense supervision and allows reuse of the controller across sensors and environments.
key_idea: Train a privileged PPO expert, freeze its latent layer and action head, then train a lightweight language-conditioned adapter on frozen VLM features to regress the expert's latent, so that navigation becomes supervised latent alignment.
insight: Aligning to the expert latent with explicit language-conditioned patch selection beats both direct action prediction (LCBC: 49.3 vs 80.5 SR in Room B) and pooled embedding alignment without token-level language conditioning (PELA: 57.6). The choice of latent layer matters sharply: d_z=256 gives 80.5 SR, while 128 and 512 give 47.0 and 46.1. Stronger frozen VLM backbones (SigLIP2 > SigLIP > CLIP) give more robustness to lighting and camera shifts with identical adapters and controller.
method: Privileged expert: a PPO MLP (obs→512→256→128→action) trained on a 159-D state (goal in body frame, velocities, 50 obstacle-cluster centroids); encoder and action head are then frozen, and the 256-D hidden layer serves as the latent z.
Frozen VLM backbone: SigLIP2-base (also CLIP, SigLIP) supplies patch-level image embeddings and a global text embedding; neither is fine-tuned.

Language-conditioned visual bottleneck (LCLAA): patches projected and passed through MHSA, an MLP scores each patch against the text embedding, a temperature softmax gives weights, and a convex sum yields a single visual token.

Query refinement: a text-derived query plus M learnable queries pass through stacked cross-attention blocks over the bottleneck token, then a sigmoid-gated fusion with the text embedding and an MLP produce ẑ.
Alignment loss: λ1·symmetric InfoNCE + (1-λ1)·MSE(ẑ,z) + λ2·||π^a(ẑ)-π^a(z)||² with λ1=0.8, λ2=1. Only the adapter is trained.
Data: 52k expert rollout steps in Room A, expanded to about 260k samples by 4 offline appearance augmentations per frame, with 8-9 templated prompts per goal; 10 epochs.
Inference: RGB and instruction go through the frozen VLM and adapter to ẑ, then the frozen action head outputs a continuous wheel velocity command.

setting.backbone: SigLIP2-base (frozen) + LCLAA adapter (trained) + frozen PPO MLP action head
setting.training_data: 52k expert rollout steps in one Isaac Sim room (Room A), augmented to ~260k image-language samples, with templated prompts
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB + templated language instruction
setting.privileged: none at test time (privileged state is used only to train the expert and to produce latent targets)

numbers_note: Custom Isaac Sim benchmark, not a standard VLN benchmark; the paper labels its OOD room as zero-shot and reports no split names. Baselines are excluded from the numbers. The privileged PPO upper bound in Room A is 97.7 SR.
results: LCLA gets 90.4 SR in-distribution and 80.5 SR zero-shot in the unseen Room B, far above LCBC (60.1 / 49.3), PELA (62.5 / 57.6) and LeLaN (61.1 / 54.8), and reduces collisions by more than 2x. It is lightweight (13M adapter parameters, ~74 ms per step) compared with LeLaN (182M, 136 ms).
limitations: Evaluated only in a single simulator, in two hand-built rooms, with templated instructions (no free-form language, long-horizon VLN, or real robot).
The frozen expert relies on simulator-derived obstacle geometry and lacks memory and planning, so it inherits the expert's limits; the latent-layer choice is very sensitive (128 and 512 fail).
No comparison on standard VLN benchmarks; loss components are not ablated, and stability analyses are only empirical.
